heteroTests Roadmap

Source: ROADMAP.md

This document tracks where the package is going. It is updated alongside meaningful code changes. Milestones are ordered, not dated. The history of what changed and why lives in NEWS.md; the statistical evidence lives in inst/validation/.

Where things stand (0.14.0)

  • On CRAN. 0.11.2 was accepted in September 2026, after one review round on 0.11.1. 0.12.0, 0.13.0 and 0.14.0 are GitHub releases: the next submission is 1.0.0 (decided 2026-10-11).
  • The validation matrix is complete for every exported perform*Test(). The sweep found six broken procedures, all corrected or withdrawn, and twenty-five of the twenty-six heteroscedasticity tests hold their nominal level (inst/validation/README.md). The tests added since have studies of their own: inst/validation/harrison-mccabe-size-power.R and inst/validation/glejser-skewed-errors.R.
  • Weighted fits were outside that matrix, and wrong. Every design in it fitted an unweighted model. On a weighted fit the tests read the raw residuals, whose variance differs across observations by assumption, and rejected a correctly weighted model every time. 0.12.0 corrects that and adds weighted designs to the matrix (inst/validation/weighted-fits-size.R). In 0.13.0 the bootstrap tests accept a weighted fit too, with designs of their own in the same study.
  • Reference equivalence is asserted to 1e-8 against lmtest, car and plm wherever a reference implementation exists. lmtest::bptest() is not a reference for weighted fits: it tests the raw residuals.
  • The public surface has been reviewed. 0.14.0 gave each of the 129 exports of 0.13.0 a verdict (the export inventory under 0.14.0): 104 are core API, 22 are deprecated and warn, and 3 move to a companion package that has no name yet. With bootstrapTestStatistic(), simulate_size() and simulate_power() the package exports 132 objects, and test-public-api.R asserts the 107 planned for 1.0.0. What stands between 0.14.0 and 1.0.0 is the interface itself, whose changes break calls (0.15.0), and the evidence and internals of 0.16.0.

What 1.0.0 means

1.0.0 is a promise rather than a feature count. From 1.0.0:

  • Exported names, argument names and order, and defaults change only in a major release, and only after a minor release in which the old form still works and warns.
  • Every exported test returns an htest object with a documented, uniform set of fields.
  • A correction to a statistic, its degrees of freedom or its p-value is a bug fix. It is never deferred for the sake of compatibility. It bumps the minor version and gets its own NEWS.md section, as 0.11.0 did.

Version numbers follow from that: a patch release changes no reported value; a minor release adds functionality or corrects a statistic; a major release breaks the API.

Everything below exists to make that promise safe to give. The sequencing rule this file has always followed still holds: statistical correctness first, then the API, and never both in one release. 0.12.0 reopened correctness for weighted fits and closed it again, and 0.13.0 corrected what was found after it, so the API is next.

Guiding principles

  • Statistical correctness first. Every test must reproduce an established reference (or a defensible derivation) and be covered by a test that checks behaviour (size and power), not just object structure.
  • A reference comparison is not a substitute for a size check. Four of the six faults the sweep found were in procedures with no reference to compare against, and the two that had one agreed with it.
  • Guards are simulated, not stored. A stored-value regression test would have frozen each of those faults rather than caught it.
  • One consistent interface. All diagnostics return base-R htest objects and follow the perform*Test(model, data, ...) convention. (Nine exported tests do not yet; see 0.15.0.)
  • Scale and robustness as first-class concerns: streaming implementations for large data, resampling and robust variants for small or non-normal samples.

Milestones

0.11.x: CRAN maintenance (now)

0.12.0: weighted fits and the shape of the variance (done)

This release was not on the roadmap. It took the 0.12.0 number because a corrected statistic bumps the minor version, and the milestones below moved up by one.

Found on the way and left for their own changes:

  • The bootstrap tests hold the weights fixed and share the error: the wild bootstrap rejects 0.086 with 150 observations and 0.105 with 600, where it rejects 0.054 and 0.048 with the true weights in the same design. A bootstrap that runs fitWLS() again on every replicate is such a correction. In the same designs it rejects 0.042 to 0.060 with 150 observations for the wild bootstrap, the White bootstrap and rbootstrap_test_statistic() with Koenker’s statistic, and 0.051 with 600 for the wild bootstrap (inst/validation/weighted-fits-size.R). Proposal, not implemented: an argument to the three functions that refits the variance function fitWLS() recorded on the model, with the same var_formula and form, in each replicate. It applies only to a fit that carries that record; weights the user supplied are known and stay fixed. See Decisions needed.

0.13.0: what was found after 0.12.0 (done)

This release was not on the roadmap either. It took the 0.13.0 number because it corrects statistics and adds functionality, and the milestones below moved up by one again.

0.14.0: review the public surface, deprecate and remove nothing (done)

Goal: every one of the 129 exports gets a verdict, which is one of core API, renamed, internal or moved out. Nothing is removed in this release. Everything that will go warns.

The author accepted the four proposals for this release on 2026-10-14: the dashboard and the benchmark suite move to a companion package and the recommendation engine stays, with its return format frozen; performCookWeisbergTest() stays, with an optional var_formula, and performNCVTest() is deprecated; test() is folded into summary.HeteroDiagnostic(); and simulate_*() and sigma_*() stay as a documented snake_case family while the one-offs are renamed. The companion package has no name yet, so the dashboard and benchmark functions are not deprecated until it has one.

    • performBreuschPaganTest() is performBPTest(), assigned at R/performBPTest.R:232.
    • performStudentizedBPTest() is a separate implementation that matches performKoenkerTest() in every column of the full sweep. Confirm the statistics agree to 1e-8, then keep one.
    • performCookWeisbergTest() delegates to performNCVTest() with the fitted values as the variance regressor. performCookWeisbergTest() becomes the one entry point for the Cook–Weisberg score test, with var_formula as an optional argument, and performNCVTest() is deprecated (decided above).
    • *Enhanced pairs: checkModel()/checkModelEnhanced(), plotResidualsFitted()/plotResidualsFittedEnhanced() and plotDiagnosticSuite()/plotDiagnosticSuiteEnhanced(). Merge each improvement into the base name.

Export inventory

Every export in NAMESPACE on 2026-10-14, with a verdict. Of the 129, 104 are core API, 10 are renamed, 12 become internal and 3 move out. The S3 methods registered in NAMESPACE are not exports and are not listed; S3method(test, HeteroDiagnostic) goes with test(). The verdicts apply the decisions of 2026-10-14 as written, and the author’s decisions on this inventory, taken the same day, are marked “decided”.

For each renamed or internal export, the last column lists every caller found by a search of R/ (code, not comments or the definition), vignettes/ and inst/validation/, adds README.md where it names the export, and counts the lines in tests/ that call it. The notebooks in inst/tutorials/ call none of these exports. The article was not searched: it moves to the 1.0 API after 1.0.0. An export that becomes internal keeps working for its callers in R/, and for the tests, which run inside the namespace; a renamed export keeps working under its old name and warns. What has to change in each pull request are the callers outside R/, and the package’s own calls of a name that will warn.

Notes on the verdicts:

  • performStudentizedBPTest() is provisional. Item 2 first asserts that it agrees with performKoenkerTest() to 1e-8 over the designs of the full sweep, weighted, rank-deficient and fitWLS() fits included. Disagreement anywhere is a finding, not a rename, and is reported before anything else.
  • test() warns and names runDiagnostics(x$model, x$data, tests), which returns what test() returns. summary.HeteroDiagnostic() keeps its return value, so no value changes in 0.14.0.
  • Registry names. "student_bp" and "ncv" stay registered and keep calling what they call now, so their output does not change. Each warns once per call of runHeteroTests() or runDiagnostics(), not once per group or bootstrap replicate, and goes in 1.0.0 with the function behind it.
  • The cache functions (cachedTest(), clearTestCache(), clearAnalysisCache()) stay exported and are not deprecated in 0.14.0. They are revisited at 1.0.0, once 0.16.0 bounds the caches.
  • rrunAdvancedDiagnostics(), runHeteroTestsParallel() and compareTestResults() stay core API. The name of rrunAdvancedDiagnostics() is still open under the item on the r-prefixed exports.
  • The simulation renames. simulate_size() and simulate_power() join the documented snake_case family, since both simulate under the sigma_*() functions.
  • bootstrapTestStatistic() takes a test function as its first argument, so it is not a perform*Test(model, data, ...); the new name says what it does in the house camelCase.
  • The dashboard and the benchmark suite are not deprecated in 0.14.0, because the companion package has no name yet. They call plotDiagnosticSuiteEnhanced(), the test factory and performNCVTest(), which change before the code moves.
  • analyzeMLResiduals() and analyseDatasetCharacteristics() spell the verb two ways. Both are core API; the roadmap names no change for them.

0.15.0: make the interface match its description

These changes break existing calls. They have to happen before 1.0.0, not after it.

    • no data argument: performArchLMTest(), performMcLeodLiTest(), performCookWeisbergTest(), performNCVTest(), performSpearmanTest(), performSpreadLevelTest(), performDavidianCarrollTest() and performHarveyTest();
    • no model argument: performBoxMTest(data, group).

    Decided on 2026-10-15 as proposed: the eight take data = NULL in second position, recovered from the model frame when omitted, and performBoxMTest() is the documented exception, since it tests the data rather than residuals. A call that passes the old second argument by position (performArchLMTest(m, 3), performCookWeisbergTest(m, ~x), performHarveyTest(m, "fitted")) is recognised by its type, works in 0.15.x, warns with the new call and stops working in 1.0.0; NEWS.md has the table. No value changes: every old and new form returns what the old form returned in 0.14.0, checked with identical() against 0.14.0. Extended on 2026-10-15 to every other test: performRESETTest(model, power) as the eight, and the 29 tests that required data now default it to NULL, the model frame. A call that worked returns what it returned, except performRESETTest(m, NULL) and performRESETTest(m, <data frame>), which read the second argument as power and returned NaN or a meaningless F.

  • Measured on 2026-10-15 in inst/validation/wild-multiplier-size.R: the cross-sectional design of Pass A at 30, 50 and 100 observations, with Gaussian, t5 and centred exponential errors, 5000 replications and B = 999, both multipliers on the same samples. The decision rule was written into the script before the full run started; the script was first committed with its results. Neither multiplier holds the level in more cells, and no paired difference is outside its 99% interval (within Monte Carlo error). Both are inside the release gate in the same six of the nine size cells, those with Gaussian and t5 errors, and outside it in the same three, those with exponential errors, where Rademacher’s multiplier rejects 0.082, 0.073 and 0.061 of the time and Mammen’s 0.078, 0.070 and 0.059: Mammen’s rate is lower in all three cells, each difference inside its 99% interval. The interval around 0.049, the rate of an exact test with B = 999, gives the same split. Against sigma^2 = exp(0.4 x1) the power of the two differs by less than one point at each n. Done (decided 2026-10-16: keep "rademacher", as the study recommended); no value changes. The help page said the bootstrap controls the size for heavy-tailed errors; that holds for the t5 errors of the study and not for the skewed ones, with either multiplier, and #125 corrected the page. A wild bootstrap without a multiplier, which may hold the level better under skewed errors, is to be measured in 0.16.0 (below).

0.16.0: statistics evidence, dependencies and internals (no API change)

    • fitWLS() keeps the original weights in the model frame of its result, so performStudentizedBPTest() on a fitWLS() fit reads stale weights: 14.81, against 1.73 for the equivalent lm(weights = estimated) fit. Suggested fix: mf[["(weights)"]] <- w in rweighted_refit(). Changes a value.
    • The single tests and performWhiteTestBootstrap() match a reordered tibble or data.table to the fit by position, through prepare_model_data_for_test(). Since 0.15.0 they refuse such data instead of returning wrong values: rcheck_data_rows(), called by rdata_or_model_frame(), compares every column of the model frame, on the rows the row names pick, with the model frame: the columns data holds under their own names value by value, and the others (log(y), log(x), poly(), ns(), offset(o), (weights), (offset)) computed from data through the predvars of the terms and the weights and offset expressions of the call. A term that depends on the rows it is computed from (I(x - mean(x)), I(x > median(x)), rank(x)), found by computing it again on half the rows, is not compared when it differs, and neither is a column that names a variable data lacks or whose computation fails; the compared columns must then leave no two rows of the fit that tie on them and differ in such a column computed from variables of data, and at least one column must be compared. The tests stop when a compared column differs, when such ties remain, when row names repeat, or when a fit with model = FALSE rebuilds a frame whose response or fitted values are not the fit’s; runHeteroTests() and runDiagnostics() do not fall back on another test for it. The model context replaces this guard, so that such data give the value on the data of the fit. Changes a value for such data. Its cost on a valid call grows with the columns it computes again: at 100,000 rows it takes about 5 ms on lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + g) and about 43 ms on a weighted fit with log() and poly() terms, against 50 to 70 ms for the Glejser and Bartlett tests and about 200 ms for Koenker’s on main. The review of 0.15.0 measured it at about a third of the Glejser (100 ms) and Bartlett (120 ms) calls at that size, before factors were compared by their codes; the model context, which reads the design from the fit, does not need it. Not covered by the guard:
      • fitWLS(data, var_formula) and performVarianceFormTest() with var_formula or against read the variables of the second formula through rvariance_frame(), which matches by name and, when no name matches and the counts agree, by position, unchecked (a reordered tibble changes their value).
      • The tests that read nothing from data (performSpearmanTest(), performHarveyTest(), performArchLMTest(), performMcLeodLiTest(), performCookWeisbergTest() without var_formula, performNCVTest(), performSpreadLevelTest(), performDavidianCarrollTest(), performVarianceFormTest() without a second formula, performRESETTest()) accept reordered data and return the value of the fit.
      • The columns a test reads besides the model (group, order_by, variable, id, time) are not compared. When every column of the model frame is compared, two rows that tie on all of them (response, regressors, weights, offset) can pass for each other, as with a binary or integer response; they then have the same design row, weight, offset and residual, so exchanging them moves only those other columns between identical observations. The review of the guard found that swapping such rows of an unweighted fit with no offset left the Bartlett, Glejser, Szroeter and GQ statistics unchanged.
      • A column computed from a vector of the workspace (weights = wvec, offset = ovec, log(x + k)) is not compared; no test reads it from data, so it needs nothing more.
      • The guard refuses data it cannot confirm, even the data of the fit:
        1. when no column of the model frame can be compared, as with lm(d$y ~ d$x); (ii) when the compared columns tie on rows of the fit that differ in a term that depends on the rows or in a term of variables of data that cannot be computed, as with a discrete response and a row-dependent regressor on the rows an na.omit fit kept (lm(score ~ g + I(x > median(x)) + z2)), or y01 ~ myf(x) after rm(myf) and ns() after detach("package:splines"). The message names the columns; pass the full data the model was fitted on, with the rows it dropped, or the variables as columns of data.
      • A term that depends on the rows is recognised by computing it again on the odd and even rows and on each half, so every row is left out of one of them; one that gives the same values on all four by chance is compared, and refused on the rows a subset = or na.omit fit kept.
      • Data that reproduce every column of the model frame exactly but are another data set, with another extra column the test reads (g in T1b of the review), give a wrong value without an error, as in 0.14.0.
      • performScatterDiagnostic() refuses a tibble in the order of the fit of a model fitted to data with character row names, which it cannot match by name.
      • cut(x, quantile(x)) in the formula makes Koenker’s test stop with “factor has new levels”, on main and with the guard alike.
      • The second review of the guard measured it at about 20 to 40% of a cheap test (Bartlett, Glejser) at 100,000 rows.
      • A model = FALSE fit whose data changed after the fit is refused by the tests that read data, with or without it, but the tests that read only the model rebuild its frame too: performRESETTest() takes its response from that frame and stays wrong, as in 0.14.0.
      • bootstrapTestStatistic() and rbootstrap_test_statistic() keep their own check (0.13.0), and the panel tests and performScatterDiagnostic() refuse data with row names of their own in another order instead of matching it by name.
      • The (weights) column is compared with the weights expression of the call computed on data. If the fitWLS() defect above is fixed by writing the estimated weights into (weights) (decision 11 of the model-context design) while the call still says weights = w, every test given data on a fitWLS() fit of a weighted model would be refused; the model context, which takes the weights from the fit, avoids it, and this guard must then skip that column for such fits.
    • The caches of runHeteroTests(use_cache = TRUE) (about 33 KB per new model) and cachedTest() (about 25 KB per call) grow without bound, as the validation cache did before #97. No value changes.
    • A multivariate lm, cbind(y, y2) ~ ..., fails with a coercion error instead of a clear refusal. No value changes.
    • The unexported performWhiteTestEnhanced(bootstrap = TRUE), through bootstrap_white_test(), takes the log of a log response twice, drops an offset given as an argument and takes rows by position. Remove it or fix it. No exported value changes.
    • About 0.8 KB per test call on a new model still persists after the validation cache is cleared, as seen in long simulations. No value changes.
    • On a rank-deficient fit (z2 = 2 * z, the design in tests/testthat/test-koenker-studentized.R) both performKoenkerTest() and performStudentizedBPTest() refuse with “Model coefficients must be finite…”, where lmtest::bptest() returns a statistic (20.87, df 2). Decide whether to compute on the estimable subspace or keep the refusal with a clearer message.
    • Move curl to Suggests: only downloadTeachingData() uses it.
    • R6 goes if TestFactory leaves the API, since it is the only user.
    • Suggests shrinks with the companion split.
    • Settle whether digest belongs in Imports or Suggests, depending on whether caching stays exported.

1.0.0: freeze

    • getting started;
    • choosing a test, turning the t5 and power tables into advice;
    • remediation;
    • theory and references.

After 1.0.0

  • First-class panel and spatial heteroscedasticity workflows.
  • Helpers that bridge detection to conditional-variance modelling (ARCH/GARCH) for the time-series path.
  • An experiment/report artefact (model-card style) summarising a diagnostic run.
  • Streaming for more tests where it is meaningful, under a single chunk_threshold_mb policy.
  • Stronger feasible-WLS and auto-transform helpers: iterated feasible GLS, an estimator of the additive variance function that keeps its fitted variances positive, and a Box–Cox search.
  • A form of performVarianceFormTest() that does not need the standardized errors to have a constant fourth moment, following the robust statistic of Wooldridge (1991).
  • A single parametrised accuracy-validation test, with reference coverage broadened to skedastic and sandwich.
  • The companion package for the dashboard and the benchmark suite (decided on 2026-10-14; not yet named).

Candidate tests

None of these is scheduled. Each would be a new export, so each has to clear the release gate in inst/validation/README.md before it ships: agreement to 1e-8 with an established implementation or with a reconstruction of the primary reference, simulated size inside the gate, and power against the alternative it is built for.

The list is arranged by where the test can be found today, because that decides both what there is to validate against and what the package would add. Availability was checked on 2026-10-09 by searching CRAN, the R documentation sites and the web for each test by name. “No R implementation found” reports that search. It is not proof that none exists.

No R implementation found

A first implementation in R. Where another system has one, it is the reference; where none does, the guard is a reconstruction of the primary reference and simulated size.

  • Modified Wald test for groupwise heteroscedasticity in a fixed-effects panel (Greene 2000; Baum 2001). The panel tests cover an individual effect and cross-sectional dependence, not unequal variances across units. Reference implementation: Stata’s xttest3. The Python package panelbox (1.0.2) has a function of that name that computes a different statistic, a likelihood-ratio form. A second search on 2026-10-10 found no R implementation either. Measured for 0.13.0 and not adopted: it does not hold its level. In the designs of inst/validation/modified-wald-size-power.R, at 5000 replications, the test as xttest3 computes it rejects a true null hypothesis at the 5% level this often:

    Errors Units T = 5 T = 10 T = 30 T = 100
    Gaussian 10 0.927 0.681 0.282 0.100
    Gaussian 30 1.000 0.966 0.584 0.183
    Gaussian 100 1.000 1.000 0.928 0.361
    t5 10 0.966 0.876 0.621 0.367
    t5 30 1.000 0.999 0.944 0.717
    t5 100 1.000 1.000 1.000 0.982

    Two unbalanced panels are at 0.809 and 1.000 under Gaussian errors. Each unit’s term is divided by a variance estimated from the same few residuals, and the excess grows with the number of units. In long panels the error reverses, because the statistic tends to a chi-squared with one degree of freedom fewer than its reference: with 2 units and 1000 periods it rejects 0.014 of the time. Three of the study’s 40 null cells fall inside the release gate, all at 300 or 1000 periods, where the two errors happen to cancel, and under t5 errors it still rejects 0.129 of the time with 10 units and 0.235 with 30 at 1000 periods. Before a test of this hypothesis can ship it needs a different variance estimate or a small-sample correction, which makes it a different test. Two leads, neither part of the study: Bartlett’s test on the within residuals held its level under Gaussian errors in an exploratory run but, being a normal-theory test, not under t5 errors; and Juhl and Sosa-Escudero (2014, Journal of Econometrics 178, 484-494) derive studentized tests for heteroscedasticity after fixed-effects estimation with the number of periods fixed, whose fit to this hypothesis has not been checked. Greene’s page 598, which Baum follows, could not be obtained, so whether Greene’s own form differs from Baum’s was not checked.

  • A joint LM test of homoscedasticity in a one-way error-component model (Baltagi, Bresson and Pirotte 2006), against heteroscedasticity in the individual effect and in the remainder error together.

  • Pagan–Hall (1983), the test of constant variance after instrumental-variables estimation, where Breusch–Pagan and White are valid only under further conditions. Reference implementation: Stata’s ivhettest. The package accepts no instrumental-variables fit today, so this one starts with the input layer.

  • Kelejian–Robinson (1998), a joint test for spatial autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity. sphet::kpjtest() is a different test by Kelejian and Piras.

  • Newey–Powell (1987), a test built on asymmetric least squares: under constant variance the expectile regressions have equal slopes. expectreg fits expectiles and has no such test.

  • Tests in nonparametric regression, which have power against any smooth departure from constant variance and need no variance regressors to be named: Eubank and Thomas (1993), Dette and Munk (1998), Zheng (2009), and Chown and Müller (2018). The cost is a bandwidth or a difference sequence to choose.

  • A consistent test of a variance function: Dette, Neumeyer and Van Keilegom (2007), Wang and Zhou (2007), and Samarakoon and Song (2011). performVarianceFormTest() has power against the terms it is given; these have it against any departure, at the cost of smoothing. Stage 1 of the first measured for 0.13.0, and not exported: as defined, it does not hold its level. The 2007 article could not be obtained; a prototype in plain R follows the authors’ submitted manuscript of 2005, whose Tables 4.1 and 4.5 it reproduces in level and to within a few points in power. In the designs of inst/validation/variance-form-size-power.R, with the variance function in one variable and the mean a linear model, the Cramér-von Mises statistic is inside the release gate in 4 of its 12 Gaussian null cells at 5000 replications, all four with constant variance at 150 or 400 observations; it rejects a true exponential or power variance function 0.019 to 0.036 of the time at 50 to 400 observations. The bootstrap draws its data from the least-squares fit of the variance function, on which the statistic’s null distribution depends: drawn from the true shape, on the same samples, three of the four such cells come to 0.047 to 0.051. Against a departure the added terms of performVarianceFormTest() do not span it has the power that test lacks, 0.750 against 0.089 at 400 observations; against the other alternatives it has less. Design note, prototype and evidence: inst/validation/variance-form-dnvk-design.md and the variance-form-dnvk-* files beside it. What to do next is under Decisions needed. Wang and Zhou (2007) assume a parametric mean, which is this package’s setting; Samarakoon and Song (2011) could not be obtained. Stage 1 of Wang and Zhou (2007) is parked on the branch feat/wang-zhou-stage1, to be resumed after 1.0.0: pass 1 of its size and power study is done, and the Gaussian null cells at 5000 replications that decide it have not been run. The branch’s wip/wang-zhou-stage1/README.md says how to resume.

  • Bai, Pan and Yin (2018), a test of homoscedasticity when the number of regressors grows with the sample. Li–Yao, below, is a different test for the same setting.

  • A design-based test of constant variance for survey data. The tests assume an independent sample with equal weights, and runSurveyHeteroTests() rejects a homoscedastic model 37% to 100% of the time when selection depends on the response or the sample is clustered. The natural candidates regress the squared residuals of a survey::svyglm() fit on the variance regressors using the design, as a Wald test (survey::regTermTest()) or as a Rao score test. Both were measured in inst/validation/survey-designs-size.R and neither clears the gate: 6% to 25% under the null at 300 and 1000 observations when the weights vary with the regressor. The variance estimate needs a small-sample correction first.

In another R package, not in this one

These add no test to R. They add it to the common interface, and each comes with a reference implementation to agree with.

  • Sign and size bias tests (Engle and Ng 1993): whether the squared residuals respond differently to negative and to positive lagged residuals. The time-series tests detect ARCH effects and say nothing about asymmetry. rugarch::signbias() computes the tests for a fitted GARCH model.
  • A break in the variance at an unknown date: the CUSUM of squares test (Brown, Durbin and Evans 1975), the statistic of Inclán and Tiao (1994), or the kappa tests of Sansó, Aragó and Carrion (2004), which stay valid under heavy tails and conditional heteroscedasticity. Goldfeld–Quandt and Szroeter need the ordering and the split to be chosen in advance. Reference implementation for the last: micss::kappa_test().
  • Simonoff–Tsai (1994) and Verbyla (1993). Versions of the Cook–Weisberg score test built on modified profile likelihood and on residual maximum likelihood, for small samples and high-leverage designs. Reference implementations: skedastic::simonoff_tsai() and skedastic::verbyla().
  • Bickel (1978) and Anscombe (1961). Tests of the variance against the fitted values. Bickel’s is the robust one. Reference implementations: skedastic::bickel() and skedastic::anscombe().
  • Li–Yao (2019) for regressions with many regressors. performHighDimensionalTest() regresses the squared residuals on principal components and cites no heteroscedasticity test as its source. Reference implementation: skedastic::li_yao().
  • A spatial Breusch–Pagan test (Anselin 1988) for fitted spatial models. performSpatialHeteroTest() applies Moran’s I to the squared residuals, which detects variance that clusters in space and does not test it against regressors. Reference implementation: spatialreg::bptest.Sarlm().
  • The rest of skedastic. Of its 25 tests, the package has counterparts for eight. Besides those named above, skedastic provides bamset(), carapeto_holt(), diblasi_bowman(), dufour_etal(), evans_king(), godfrey_orme(), honda(), horn(), rackauskas_zuokas(), wilcox_keselman(), yuce() and zhou_etal(). None is a priority by itself; each is a candidate when a user asks for it.

Order of work

The first group is where the package can contribute something R does not have, which is also what a reader of the article asks of it. Within that group:

  1. The modified Wald test. The panel functions exist, and it is the test Stata users look for under the name xttest3. Measured for 0.13.0 and not adopted, because it does not hold its level (above).
  2. The Dette, Neumeyer and Van Keilegom test. It removes the main limitation of performVarianceFormTest(), and is the most work of the two. Stage 1 done for 0.13.0: as the manuscript defines it, it does not hold its level when the variance is not constant (above).

Done

  • A Glejser test that is valid under skewed errors (Im 2000; Machado and Santos Silva 2000), in 0.13.0, as performGlejserTest(robust = TRUE). In the designs of inst/validation/glejser-skewed-errors.R the uncorrected statistic rejects a true null hypothesis 9% to 18% of the time at the 5% level when the errors are skewed, at every sample size, and skedastic::glejser() uses the uncorrected absolute residuals as well. The corrected statistic is the default since 0.15.0 (the 0.15.0 milestone, above).
  • Harrison–McCabe (1979), in 0.13.0, as performHarrisonMcCabeTest(), beside Goldfeld–Quandt and Szroeter. The 1979 article was not read; the definition rests on Harrison (1981), by its first author, whose published exact critical values the function reproduces, and on lmtest::hmctest(), with which the statistic agrees to 1e-8. The p-value is exact under normal errors given the regressors. Neither reference computes that p-value: lmtest::hmctest() simulates it from a regression on a constant alone, and skedastic::harrison_mccabe() 2.0.3 drops repeated eigenvalues and, with deflator, leaves the design in the order of the rows. In the designs of inst/validation/harrison-mccabe-size-power.R it holds its level under Gaussian errors, rejects 12% to 16% of the time under t5 errors as the other two ordered tests do, and has less power than either.

Decisions needed

Question Proposal Needed by
Bootstrap tests on a fitWLS() fit Add an argument to performWildBootstrapTest(), performWhiteTestBootstrap() and bootstrapTestStatistic() that runs fitWLS() again in each replicate, on by default when the model records a variance function. Holding the weights fixed, the wild bootstrap rejects 0.086 and 0.105 at 150 and 600 observations; estimating them again, 0.060 and 0.051; with the true weights, 0.054 and 0.048. Postponed on 2026-10-12: 0.13.0 accepts a weighted fit in these functions and holds the weights of a fitWLS() fit fixed in each replicate, so a default that estimates them again changes values 0.13.0 returned, and has to be announced in bold in a minor release. Moved from 0.14.0 on 2026-10-14: the new default changes a default and the values these functions return, which belongs with the other default changes of 0.15.0, not in 0.14.0, where no value may change 0.15.0
Ties in the ordering of performSzroeterTest() Average the ranks within ties and adjust the null variance for them. Today ties keep the order of the rows the model was fitted to, which holds the level but makes the statistic depend on that order when order_by is discrete, and for the registered test on a model whose design rows repeat, as with factors, binary or other discrete regressors. It changes the values the function returns 0.16.0
